utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, can you hear me in a thank that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good morning, Your Honours and my apologies for keeping you waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem, Ms. Korner. Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with Milan Trbojevic, my co-counsel and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you too. Are there any preliminaries before we admit the witness? I just wanted to inform you with regard to what was mentioned yesterday about the Halilovic transcript that the exercise is ready. I will go through it again just to make sure that nothing has been overlooked and then a decision will be given later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should make it clear, in the light of the ruling, on those days we were working on summaries so all you've got, Mr. Ackerman, is a summary of the relevant evidence. We didn't feel that any of it was Rule 68 as we said, but if required, we can of course give you the full version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Once more, could you please repeat your solemn declaration to tell us the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Mr. Ackerman will be concluding his cross-examination of you this morning. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How are you this morning? Are you okay?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to start this morning with a section that I have headed, "The Prijedor authorities operated independently." And my first question of you in that regard was, it's true, is it not, that at times, the local SDS in Prijedor ignored directives from SDS Sarajevo and blocked things for which they had received orders from Sarajevo? That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly. Only at the first stage of the SDS activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When I ask you that question, I'm referring to your testimony in case IT-97-24-T of 8 July, 1998 at page 369, line 21, when you said, "And when it comes to Prijedor the SDS did not fully follow the directives from the SDS office in Sarajevo. Very often they would block the implementation of certain things for which they had orders." That's what you said in that case. Didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I said exactly that it refers only -- that it held true only of the early days of the SDS when the President was Mr. Srdic and a little later at the time when they were distributing offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, after the takeover of Prijedor and the creation of the Serbian government in Prijedor, that continued. They ignored matters coming from Sarajevo and ignored matters coming from ARK also, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was no longer keeping abreast with the SDS activities at the time that you are talking about, that is when they took over the power or rather when they set up their parallel authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like to you look at a document, P1268, please. What you have there is the Official Gazette of Prijedor municipality, date of Thursday, 25 June, 1992, and each of the decisions has an identifying number and what I'd like you to do is -- it's down toward the very end, I believe, is to find decision number 116.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you mean towards the end of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Itself? Yes. Then I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The particular conclusion is dated 23 June, 1992, and indicates that it -- that the original was signed by Dr. Milan Kovacevic. This conclusion reads as follows, does it not: "The Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality does not accept and considers invalid all decisions by the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina adopted before 22 June, 1992."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, could you slow down, please, because our ELMO screen does not work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was about to say I can't actually find -- I'm sorry, it's our fault, but I can't find the particular decision he's looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I don't have it either. In fact I was going to see whether we could have it on the ELMO. This is a document to which reference has been made before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right but it's not -- for some reason, we go in the copies we've got, and Mr. Ackerman has obviously this time done better than us, it goes decision, the last page is 115 and 119 and the one before that is 118 and 117.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As Your Honour will recall, this is the document that the Prosecution chose to translate only parts of and we then provided the translations of other parts so it would have been a separate -- it became part of P1268, but I think we provided the translation of these extra parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't have it here. Not in --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We don't have it at all and as somebody has pointed out, the ELMO doesn't appear to be working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It's -- mine is power management off. It's working now but there is nothing on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is no document. Is there a copy that we could put on the ELMO? Thanks very much. And perhaps if Mr. Ackerman would be kind enough -- for some reason we all appear to have not had this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the reason I think is what has just been explained by Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the number is 116, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, 116. And it's now very clear on the ELMO, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I've referred to the first paragraph there, sir. The second paragraph reads, "The Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality shall implement all enactments submitted to and adopted after 22 June, 1992, by the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region." Now, that's what that document indicates; correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And clearly what they are saying is that we didn't -- we don't accept any of the authority of the Autonomous Region of Krajina before 22 June, 1992. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what it says, yes, one could make -- draw such a conclusion. But I cannot tell you because I was not making part in any of the developments so that I cannot really tell you how the authorities in Prijedor and around it functioned. I can make some conclusions. I can make conjectures on the basis of what I've read, but I do not have any real knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, we'll look at another document and I'll give this one to the usher too. It's the same packet, sir. It's decision number 119.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You both have that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We'll put it on the ELMO anyhow so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, this document is a couple of days later. The first one we looked at was the 23rd of June. This one is two days later, the 25th of June, and paragraph 1 of this one reads as follows, does it not? "The Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality shall not implement enactments adopted by the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina until the assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina has elected all members of the government respecting the principle of equal representation of municipalities through the election of their candidates for members of the government." So having said in the first one that they would implement decisions after 22 June by 25 June, they are again indicating rejection of the authority of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, are they not?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what the text says, and it is obviously the basis for the request that their members be incorporated in the Krajina authority. It seems to me like a struggle for power, but my only comment can be the same as the one that I gave you to your previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree with you about the power struggle analysis. I think you're right about that. In the Stakic case, on 18 June, 2002, you were shown another document during the examination by Ms. Korner, and I'd ask that you take another look at it. It's P1272. And I think -- I'm suggesting this is just an example of how the authorities in Prijedor were ignoring decisions of ARK. This is a decision of the ARK Crisis Staff dated 10 June of 1992, and it talks about the immigration from ARK of children, women and old men?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not in this one, I'm afraid, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, Mr. Ackerman, this is not the one 172 that I have. The Exhibit P1272 is a decision, a ruling, of the president of the executive committee of the municipality of Prijedor appointing a particular person to a particular position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I wonder what this is that I have, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you tell us the Stakic number we can probably tell you what the P number is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can't even do that much. I can't do a disclosure number. It's 229 is the disclosure number, 2.29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That 2.29 is also the disclosure number of this 1272 that I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then there is a reference 0063/3986, at the top, right corner. And that's in the B/C/S original, which is also marked "confidential."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it's a mystery that I think I'm probably incapable of solving, Your Honour, so what I will do is hand the English to the usher to put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there some kind of reference number on it apart from 2.29?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it has some numbers from my own document system. It has --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just tell me the date again of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The date of the document is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 10 June, he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 10 June, 1992. It's actually two documents in one. It's -- let me just have the usher show it to you, Ms. Korner, rather than trying to describe it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have that document. That document that I have is dated the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the Stakic number might be 150B. What Ms. Korner said --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 240. Yes, that's it. P240. 12th of June. It's actually, yes, from the Banja Luka Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Can I have mine back? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What we have here, sir, is a communication from the security services centre in Banja Luka. That's the police station, the CSB, to -- apparently sent to Prijedor, enclosing a decision of the ARK Crisis Staff. And that decision speaks of the immigration of children, women and old men, and says in paragraph 2, "Activities related to the above shall be carried out in cooperation with humanitarian societies." Now, in the Stakic case, Ms. Korner asked you if this was being done in cooperation with humanitarian organisations and you said no, it was not. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, there was no cooperation with humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. So this is another -- it's just an example of how Prijedor was paying no attention to what was going on in the ARK Crisis Staff or the Autonomous Region of Krajina in June of 1992, in accordance with that other decision we saw dated the 23rd; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is how you read it, it may look like it, but what I know is from Banja Luka, that is from the centre of the regional government, still people did not leave through humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. That's the point. Now, I'd like you to look at a document P269, please. This document, P269, sir, comes from the Official Gazette of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina of 30 June, 1992. It's a decision of 10 June, 1992, signed by Dr. Radovan Karadzic. And the particular part of that that I want to draw your attention to is Article 5, "War commissions shall be formed within 15 days of the date this decision enters into force. The day the war commissions are formed Crisis Staffs shall cease to operate in municipalities across the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, that would indicate that there should be a war commission in Prijedor by the 25th of June, and that the Crisis Staff should cease to operate. That did not happen, did it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was physically not abreast of the changes in the Serb government, and the relationship between the local and higher authorities so that I cannot really know what was going on. Possibly that is how it was or perhaps it wasn't like that, but I do not really have any knowledge about that because this makes reference to June, 1992, plus 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you do know --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which makes it -- so it -- July, 1992, and I've already explained to you the situation that I was in during the previous month and at that time, so that I can make some inferences on the basis of what I'm reading here, but I know nothing about the context, so that it is very difficult for me to make any definite conclusions on the basis of such a text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you do know, don't you, that the Crisis Staff in Prijedor continued to operate in July? You know that, don't you? If you don't, say so. That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've told you, about the time indicated here, which is the 24th of June onward, I didn't have that kind of information. Towards the end of July, I was arrested and after that, I obviously could not have any information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that question, Mr. Ackerman. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm finished with that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: New subject, Mr. Sejmenovic, I want to talk to you for a moment about the plebiscite conducted by the SDS in the fall of 1991. You remember that as having occurred in November of 1991, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that the plebiscite took place at about that time but I do not remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your testimony in cause IT-97-24-T, 8 July, 1998 at page 389, you said this about that plebiscite, "I have to stress that we at the parliament could not accept such a kind of plebiscite because it was not constitutional. It was not legal. One could never hold a plebiscite for only one segment of the population." Could you tell us how it was illegal? What law was it that that plebiscite violated?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You have to ask lawyers, experts, about that period of Bosnia and Herzegovina's functioning. I presented to you the position taken by the parliament and that was taken on the basis of many discussions and expert opinions and interpretations of the then constitution. I am not qualified to go into such details and to elaborate on the legal aspect of individual provisions of the constitution and law. So that was the official position of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted by a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you're testimony that it was illegal was not based upon anything you knew about it being illegal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has already answered that question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On the same day, 8 July, 1998, you just told us that you don't know anything about the law or that you don't know the law and therefore you can't tell us why that was not legal. On that same day, at page 445 of the transcript, you were asked a question, "Based on your knowledge of the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would it be normal for the President of an executive committee to give a direction to a military commander of a JNA unit?" That question was objected to on the ground that you had no expertise in law and had not been qualified as an expert on law. Mr. Keegan then asked you a number of questions to qualify you as an expert on the law. He asked you about how you had to become very familiar with the law in your duties as a member of parliament. You indicated, yes, it was important for that. Quoting from you, "As a member of the parliament of the republic, I had to discuss proposals, drafts of the law, participate in these discussions. We adopted several hundreds of amendments to already-existing laws. Members of Parliament are not exclusively lawyers." And then he went on to ask you another question about your knowledge of the law, you again said, "Yes, we discussed that." And then Judge May decided that there was sufficient evidence that you could be qualified as a legal expert and could answer the question about the law. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, and I stand by it, but the previous question was constitutional subject matter, and you being a good lawyer, are aware of the weight of such matter and it is indeed something that should be dealt with by experts. So it -- this other thing had to do with the actual functioning of government at lower levels, or participation in and observation of government, and on that basis, a lot could be learned about the mechanisms of how government functioned, but the constitution and its related subject matter is something I did not go into. So I respect the views of experts who are involved in such matters, and who were engaged by parliament too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it your position that it -- then, that it is illegal for a political party to try to make a determination regarding the feelings of its supporters on an important issue by asking them their opinions? Do you think that's illegal?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I used the expression "illegal," I don't know whether it was interpreted very well, but what is legal is what the assembly, as the highest organ of legislative government adopted. What was done politically speaking, and what was not approved by parliament, is something that we can call illegal, unlawful. That's what it's all about. Certain actions were taken on the basis of existing laws or in accordance with parliamentary approval and the other hand there were things that were not approved by parliament. That's what I referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, a political party, independent of the government, has its own rules, regulations, laws, if you will, and can function independently as a political party, and can ask its members, "Do you agree with this proposition or not?" There is nothing illegal about that, is there? Wouldn't it make sense for the SDA to try to find out what their members feel about something so they can take a position that reflects those feelings?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think your microphone is on, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have understood you, sir. That is the mechanism of the functioning of the party. Ultimately the majority views are the views of the party. Also in parliament, there is position and opposition and there is a struggle of different views and the view that prevails is accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we move to another subject and another question, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, we are doing that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we are wasting our time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your testimony in the Stakic case, talking about the arming of Serbs in the Prijedor area, at page 4545, you said that, "Military units in the Prijedor area were being additionally armed," and were you asked where those additional arms for the military units were coming from. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that we talked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In answer to where the additional armaments came from, you said this: "Warehouses full of ammunition and combat materiel were set up in several places in the Prijedor municipal area, so all these were elements of what I referred to as additional arming by the 5th Kozara Brigade and other new elements coming in." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that that is what I said verbatim, but I did say something to that effect and I agree with what you've just read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What were those places that were set up? Where were these warehouses full of ammunition and combat materiel. Tell us where they were?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found out from some people that at the Prijedor garrison, some depots were made. Also we found out from non-Serb officers who were within the 5th Kozara unit for a while that big warehouses, big depots and big training grounds were opened somewhere between Prijedor and Sanski Most in a forest. That's what I heard from a specific person who was not a rank and file soldier. I think this person was a Lieutenant and this person deserted. There were a few artillery batteries with ammunition, where the weapons were deployed, although beforehand, there were never in such places. For example, behind the village of Cejreci in the area of Tomasica, also at Kozara in Benkovac I heard that there was a large number of soldiers it would arrived there and that weapons were being brought up there too. I'm saying this because in Prijedor, before the war, when the situation was normal, there was only this one small military garrison in Prijedor. And there were no big military units or facilities, at least as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I would like to make sure that you understand that I'm asking you a rather precise question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that is the case, Mr. Ackerman, and this is what I was going to suggest before he started answering the question. If you want to go into details and expect the witness to go into details, then I suggest we bring out a detailed map of the Prijedor region or municipality and he starts pinpointing one place after the other so that we have a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. clear picture. If that is what you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That probably makes sense, Your Honour. Let me ask him a preliminary question first because it may waste time if I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm specifically referring to your statement in the Stakic trial that reads as follows: "Warehouses," that's plural, "Warehouses full of ammunition and combat materiel were set up in several places in the Prijedor municipal area." Now, if I were to give you a map, could you show us on that map where each of these warehouses, plural, is located that you contend were full of ammunition and combat materiel. Could you show us on the map where those warehouses were?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. According to what I was told, what was conveyed to me, that is, I can, yes. Approximately of course. Not with precision, not the exact localities, but I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, now when you answered that question the first time I asked you, you started referring to artillery batteries. Artillery batteries are not warehouses and I'm asking you about warehouses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait before you answer because he also suggested that where there were artilleries there were ammunition depots, where a new troops or units arrived, ammunition depots were created. That was the gist of his answer. What I would suggest if we are going to go into details if you feel it is necessary to go into details, then we identify a map that can be used for the purpose of this question and his answer and we proceed accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm willing to do that. I just don't know the exhibit number of an appropriate map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps Ms. Gustin could help us here. Which Prijedor map would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Ms. Sutherland is probably the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We think P1127 may be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have a look at it first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful to the Prosecutor for that assistance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can help because I know that the Registrar is not normally in this Court, although she's familiar with the Prijedor area. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's probably good. Show it to the witness and see if it will work for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we have a spare copy of that map or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can give Your Honours a black and white one, a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't need a colour -- what I asked for is a copy to be used by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, he's going to be on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can he mark on that one?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we can use a black and white one rather than --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he can have the black and white.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. Give the witness a black and white. And if necessary, we'll ask him to mark, put markings on it, and then it will be made into an exhibit. If it's too complicated for you, Mr. Sejmenovic, because I see that this is quite a detailed map, but if it is too complicated for you, we'll try and find a simpler map. At the moment is focusing on Prijedor, the town of Prijedor, and perhaps we can start from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We are looking at the town of Prijedor now on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Usher give the witness a coloured pen, preferably red or green, and ask him to put marks. What I would suggest you do first, Mr. Sejmenovic, is, since the question mainly dealt with warehouses, warehouses full of ammunition, you indicate on that map the spots, the localities, as near as possible where these warehouses were situated. And we start with those first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the town of Prijedor itself, there was the army garrison building. As the 5th Kozarska unit was withdrawing from the front line in Croatia, quantities of ammunition were brought in that were stored somewhere within the garrison compound. That is somewhere in this area here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can I ask you to put GP against that circle that you have marked on that map, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, not -- leave it GP for -- GP1, GP1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like to ask a question before we go to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, what you're saying is that this ammunition warehouse that you identify in that location existed because the 5th Kozara Brigade had withdrawn from the fighting in Croatia back to Prijedor; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of this, that is to say all this ammunition and artillery pieces were put there after the 5th Kozarska unit returned from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so what the materiel that you're referring to is what they brought back with them from the battlefields in Croatia; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know if they brought all that materiel from the battlefield. As for this one enormous depot that I already referred to and that the Lieutenant told me about, the Lieutenant who deserted, that is -- I have to keep moving the map so that I could show you the right direction. So it was here in the direction of Sanski Most. So the road leading to Ljubija and then further on, and further on in this direction, so I'm going to put an arrow on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, it has been marked as GP2 in a circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then with an arrow pointing somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How far off that map would that GP2 actually be?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. So it's the direction towards Sanski Most. To pinpoint it a bit more precisely, I think it's around the village of Rasavci, according to what the Lieutenant said. And indeed there were enormous quantities of weapons there, artillery, ammunition, ammunition for multiple rocket launchers, et cetera. In my opinion, he saw there the kind of weapons that he never saw in Croatia. That is with Mr. Salih Elezovic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You never saw that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you say that he said something about those being the kind of weapons he never saw in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ammunition, ammunition. Calibres, the calibres he saw there he had never seen at the front line. He did not see the ammunition for the so-called VBR, the multiple rocket launchers, whereas, over there he did see stored shells for multiple rocket launchers and they looked very imposing because the calibres are very big.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any idea why the JNA would be uninterested in using the best weaponry they had available in the battle in Croatia? Does that make any sense to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think the witness is being asked to speculate here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what he's doing anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know. You're inviting him to do it, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Ms. Korner's objection is sustained. One can draw conclusions, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Show us another warehouse, will you? Show us the third warehouse full of ammunition and combat materiel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to answer the previous question. Just proceed to indicate the third warehouse. Or where you believe the third warehouse was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We found out that in the area of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Urije there were artillery pieces that were deployed and also that there was ammunition by these artillery pieces. I am referring to artillery pieces, long-range howitzers, as they told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, when you say, "We found out," you're using that word "we" again which means you didn't find out but somebody else did; right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received reports from the field. "We" in the party. Or rather "we" in the group of municipal officials were informed by persons who observed this, who noticed this. If you insist, I will stop using this type of expression and I will only refer to what I personally saw, but I am not doubting many of the facts that we were informed of from persons who came and told us about these facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. It's not a question of who insists or who doesn't insist here, Mr. Sejmenovic. You have every right to say "we" if you mean the party and Mr. Ackerman has every right also to have you clarify what you mean when you use the expression "we." But you have every right to, and we also want to know what you in the plural, collectively as the party, gathered by way of intelligence, by way of information. So could you mark that third circle with GP3, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what was there at GP3, did you say? Another warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were guns there, cannons with ammunition, with large quantity of ammunition. In normal conditions, ammunition is never placed by cannons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And where -- where in this Urije was this located? Was it located in a -- I don't know. Tell me, where it was it located in Urije?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know of any other warehouses?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had received information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "We" being not you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I did not tour the area to see whether there were warehouses or artillery pieces there or not. After all, you couldn't just go around these areas just like that, those that already had military security. Put an arrow here because we received information that somewhere behind the village of Cejreci. I don't know in which area this was exactly -- but here it is, GP4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you encircle that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You keep speaking about "we" received information and I just want to make sure that every time you use the word "we" you mean it's something that you yourself have no knowledge about. You're only talking about what you heard from others. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's made that clear already, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, there was a time, Your Honour, where he said "we" did include him. I don't know how we are going to sort out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When the moment comes, Mr. Sejmenovic, when "we" includes also you personally, firsthand knowledge, then if you are using the preposition "we," please do tell us also that "we" means also "I" personally included, came about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Came about this information or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have -- we have a really big problem here with this language situation because you have as evidence an exhibit that is all of his testimony in the Stakic case. And throughout that, he uses this word "we." And anybody that's ever studied language, any language, knows that "we" includes you. You don't say "we" unless you mean yourself as part of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sometimes "we" means only "I."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sometimes it can, but it never means they. It never means they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it's being used --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I assist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it's being used in a very misleading way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I assist? If it assists, Mr. Ackerman, we've always had this problem with witnesses from Bosnia, the difficulty of sorting out what they themselves saw and what they were told. But if it helps with Mr. Sejmenovic - can I put it this way - I'm perfectly content to proceed on the basis that "we," when used by him in the transcript for Stakic, he's 90 per cent likely not to have been him personally but he's been told it, so that it's not direct evidence. I think from memory and from rereading the transcript, it's pretty clear where he's talking about events he directly saw himself, but I am not going to try and persuade Your Honours at any stage that where "we" is used, it means direct evidence from what he himself saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not taking it like that any way. So I fully agree. Please in the course of your testimony or what's left of it, when you use the term "we", if you want to assist us better, in all those cases where "we" means also "I" included, came by this information, then please do tell us. What is firsthand knowledge in your case and not just information acquired by a group to which you belonged at the time, please do make the distinction, because that would be very helpful. And at the end of your testimony, I will ask you a very direct question with regard to your testimony in Stakic, if you could identify for us those particular instances that you were present at and that you can recall personally, without going into details, so that we make a very clear distinction as to what you came to know personally and what you were told or what you heard as a result of your political connections or standing at the time, and involvement, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Sir, are there more warehouses? Are you finished or are there more?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of Tomasica, I'm trying to locate Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: GP5, that should be, because you have already put GP4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So somewhere in the area of Tomasica. That was the information I received. Then in the area --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what was there in that area of Tomasica, according to the information you received?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Artillery and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And who did you receive that information from?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when we agreed that I would not say "we" any more but rather "I," I knew we would find ourselves in this predicament. I cannot now recall the name of the person who gave me this information or many other pieces of information because there -- it was very -- there was very lively activity and there was a lot of information. Some are easy to remember and I remember them, but this was information that was submitted either to the party or perhaps some officials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No one is going to blame you, Mr. Sejmenovic, if ten years after those events you do not remember a name here and a name there, especially when it comes to intelligence gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When did you learn this information?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember the date but it must have been a few days after artillery had been put in place and ammunition transported there. I can give you the name of the concrete person in this particular case, that is, about two such cases. As for the remaining three, I can't. I learned this from a local official in the neighbourhood community of Cela, Mr. Mehmet Mesic, because he has some private property in that area, Cela, that is, Gomjenica is an area which is adjacent to the area of Tomasica Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and from people who lived there, we -- I received this information and it was the secretary of the neighbourhood community responsible for national defence, who was told that by Mr. Mehmet Mesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Are there more?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you have marked to GP5 now. You said, expect another three or something like that, if you could mark them, please. You have already told us that you don't remember the name of the informer, but perhaps you do remember the details as to what kind of warehouses they were, what they contained, in other words, what kind of ammunition was stored there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the area of Benkovac, I'm trying to locate it but I can't. Oh, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You marked GP6. What's at GP6?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: GP6, before the war, there were some military facilities there, some structures. At this time, there were troops quartered there who also had their weapons and people saw that and told the either party or municipal officials that in addition to troops, weapons were also being amassed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't it the case that the troops there had come there for a rest from the fighting in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why they had come, why they came, I do not know. Nobody told me. And as far as I can remember, I don't think that our local or municipal officials were officially informed about it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you finished yet or do you have more? Is there a GP7?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt that in -- there are two locations more. There were also some in the direction towards Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What did you mark there, GP what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: GP7.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay, GP7?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: GP7.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tell us very quickly, what it was your understanding was located at GP7?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I heard, there were also some artillery pieces and multi-barrelled rocket launchers targeting Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know who you heard that from and when?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is there another one? Is there a GP8?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that there was something in the quarry above Kozarac, a gun, but I did not hear of any significant quantity of weapons or ammunition. I've heard of only one gun being there so that perhaps I shouldn't include that. It is also possibly that there were some other locations, but I do not remember them right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. We need to have that marked as DB number 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, usher, please, because he needs to sign that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It will be DB115, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: DB115 will be the exhibit number, yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's got a Stakic exhibit number on it at the moment so it needs to be crossed through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, obliterate it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As a matter of sheer interest, your honour, what does GP stand for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Initially it was going to be garrison something, then I decided it was going to be gunpowder. I knew you were going to ask that question, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, has learned to read my mind after all this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: After a quarter of a century being a Judge, I have learned to read minds. So I was prepared for your question. GP means gunpowder. Yes. As I haven't seen the witness signing the page, sign it either at the top or at the bottom, please. Not there because -- in the middle-- yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And that will be admitted, it will be admitted as Exhibit DB115?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I want to go back to your testimony in answer to that question of arming. The very next sentence, you said, "At the same time we noticed that weapons were being distributed to Serb civilians in certain villages." And again that "we noticed" means that you didn't see any weapons being distributed to Serb civilians in certain villages, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. In the wake of that incident, Mr. Muhidin Cepic came with that information. He was a member of the local party branch who had watched the scene with another man and he was very upset when he came to the party premises and told us to call municipal officials, to call the press, to go to -- record it on tape and do something about it. So it was Mr. Muhidin Cepic who provided that information about the distribution of weapons in Cirkin Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, just a sentence later, I think, you say this: "Automatic rifles were being distributed to civilians and around the houses in the village. Helicopters came down and left crates in certain places, crates carrying as we assumed, weapons. There was in Petrov Gaj bordering on the Omarska area. It also occurred in the hamlet Sajaci, near Trnopolje." Now when you say there "it also occurred," does it mean that it also occurred that helicopters came down?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sajaci.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it mean, when you say "It also occurred in the hamlet Sajaci," do you mean that helicopters came down and left crates in certain places there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally saw helicopters land in nearby hamlet, Sajaci, because it's not far from my house, but people from the neighbourhood community, from the local authorities, in Sajaci asked what's happened, and they could see that something was being unloaded. Yet they were given a bizarre explanation, denying of course that there was anything unloaded from that helicopter, and I can give you that explanation, if you want me to. That there was a soldier in this helicopter and that they had landed to partake of coffee in his house. That was the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to understand exactly what it was you were saying here in Stakic. You said, "Helicopters came down and left crates." And then you say, "That occurred in the hamlet Sajaci and I witnessed that latter occurrence myself." And the impression I got from reading that was that you saw a helicopter land in Sajaci and unload crates. Would I be wrong in assuming that that's what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're wrong. All I saw was the landing itself, and it did land, some 20 minutes later or so, as far as I can remember, it took off again and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And where is Sajaci?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 400 metres away from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your house would be in Trnopolje; right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the story that you were given by officials from that area when you were -- when asked about it was that it was a soldier who had stopped by to have coffee with his family. That's what the story you got; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I heard in the neighbourhood community offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you said, based upon having seen a helicopter land and having been told that it was so a soldier could have coffee with his family, that that combination of things convinced you that that helicopter was distributing weapons to the Serbs in that hamlet; correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The explanation that we were given simply made no sense, because it simply can't be that a helicopter lands for a plain soldier. To begin with, just ordinary foot soldiers seldom were entitled to helicopter flights and certainly not just to have a meal or something. It won't land for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What if that soldier was a Lieutenant Colonel? That would make a difference, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is something that I don't know, but what we were told by Mr. Hadzic from a village near Omarska that people had seen with their own eyes, as they worked in their field, how that helicopter landed and how they were unloading two large crates from that helicopter and take them towards Omarska so we could not but put two and two together in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If what you just said, which you haven't said before, is somebody witnessed crates being unloaded from that particular helicopter, you never said that before, if what you just said just now is true, then it would make no sense for you to consult the competent officials from that hamlet to tell you what was going on, because you would have seen it. So you just made that up just now, didn't you? Sitting there, you just made that up, that people had seen crates being unloaded.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, sir. No, sir. This was something -- this was the news in Kozarac. Everybody talked about it, and it was not very pleasant when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know a family that lives there by the name of Milutinovic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some Milutinovics, but I do not recall knowing personally any one of them. There were a number of Milosevics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Don't you know that Milan Milutinovic was a Lieutenant Colonel in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You never saw any weapons being distributed to Serb civilians in the Prijedor area by anyone, did you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said it. Personally, I did not see it. I was not physically present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In -- I'm going to another subject now. Yeah, we can do that. You had a meeting in mid-May in Prijedor with SDS representatives. I think it was around somewhere between the 16th and 18th of May. Do you remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the latter half of May? Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was the meeting that Becir Medunjanin attended, that you attended and so forth; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And at that meeting the SDS representatives there were demanding that the Muslims in the Kozarac area surrender a certain discrete number of weapons, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Different numbers were mentioned but they requested that huge amounts of weapons, quantities of weapons, be surrendered, not only the SDS but also the troops, the officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think sometimes you've said 5.000, sometimes 7.000, I'm not going to argue with you about that. It was a large number of weapons, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you -- your group, not necessarily you, but people in your group, at least, tried to make it clear that the Muslims in Kozarac didn't have anywhere near that number of weapons, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. Mr. Becir Medunjanin was -- had the largest number of interventions at that meeting and was saying -- was saying about what the real state of affairs was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what I think was probably clear to you was that what was really being demanded was that Kozarac be turned into a Serb-administered village. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not the demand made at that meeting. They requested the surrender of those several thousand pieces of weaponry, and that was the prerequisite for everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But also discussed at that meeting was the issue of the Serb flag and the Serb insignia on the police uniforms, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simo Miskovic, the SDS president had something to say about that, but the main say was with the officers. He did mention something that there were some extremists, that those extremists could not bear to see any other symbols but Serbs. That is about the vein in which Miskovic spoke. But what was repeated several times was that some huge quantities of weapons had to be turned over, which however did not exist, and of course, threats were being addressed with the weaponry that the army had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so Medunjanin then finally said that he would convey their messages to the people of Kozarac and let the people of Kozarac decide what they wanted to do, whether they wanted to surrender weapons, accept the Serb flag, and the Serb police insignia, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He did say something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in closing, said, "We will inform you later about the decision. I only guarantee that no Muslim will fire a single shot at any Serb. And please do not attack because there is no reason to attack." That's what he said, right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and repeated it. We were all saying that, and that was the thrust of the activity, not to provoke it in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was simply not true, was it? In fact, the first shots fired were Muslims shooting at Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the version of the Serb army, but to be quite honest, I don't believe it. I believe that the Serb troops were bent upon creating some kind of provocation or setting the stage for a provocation so that then they would have the excuse to attack the other side. That is what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it would be an appropriate time for a break now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Ackerman. Let's have a break of 25 minutes, resuming immediately after.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, sir, we are going to do -- okay. We are going to do a different subject now. I want to go to some testimony you gave in the Stakic case. I'm referring now to page 4577. You were asked this question, "Did the army take decisions involving, for example, defence or anything to do with military manoeuvres without involvement of the political authorities?" In part, your answer was as follows, "The army did not take orders from civilian structures at a lower level. The general staff was the only authority to issue orders or the lower ranking military command structures." That's what you said; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how the army operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. And further you said, "As far as direct orders concerning military directives and weapons were concerned, civilians could never order anything like that." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except for the Supreme Commands of course, but as far as lower levels are concerned, that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And that was the -- that was the way the JNA had operated for years and years and years, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in principle, that's the way it was, as far as I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to ask you if you know -- I'm on a different subject again now -- you spoke a little bit about Celinac events at the very beginning of your testimony the other day. I just wanted to know if you know what happened to the Muslim people who lived in Celinac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know about the survivors, the Muslim refugees who survived, and who came from Bosanska Vrbanja. I heard a few things from these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that there are still -- that there is a very large number of Muslim people living in Celinac today? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that quite a few Muslims returned to many parts of Republika Srpska. This return process is a rather intensive one and it is still under way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that many remained there throughout the whole war?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which number is involved. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that some of the Muslim men from Celinac even served in the Army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Celinac, but I know that a symbolical number for a variety of reasons remained in the former JNA which was later turned into the Army of Republika Srpska but this is a very small number of people, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm getting real close to the end, Mr. Sejmenovic, and there are some just sort of miscellaneous little matters that I would like to go through and I hope we can do it with, you know, rather quickly. In the Stakic case, page 4526, you're talking about that period of time when Muhamed Cehajic was the President of the Prijedor municipality and Milomir Stakic was the vice-president. And the question I want to ask you about that was: Based upon your understanding of how a municipality government operates, was the vice-president somebody who could exert exactly the same powers as the President could or was he somehow subordinate to the president?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vice-president was supposed to deputise for the President if the President could not conduct sessions of the assembly. If he was absent, if he was sick, then he would take over all the powers of president. However, if both are present, what the direct legal relationship is is something I don't know. That is prescribed by the Statute of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next subject, you were testifying about military persons attending municipal assembly meetings and at page 4533 you said that "In one of those meetings at least the military people talked about the need --" I'm quoting now starting with "the need" is a quote from you, sir. "The need to send Prijedor residents to the battlefield in Croatia for the purpose of defending or protecting the town of Prijedor." Can you tell us what that means? And why would it be important for Prijedor residents to go to Croatia to defend or protect Prijedor? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you read out just now is not a verbatim interpretation of what I said but that is the gist of it. Colonel Arsic spoke about that on several occasions, and he claimed that Prijedor is defended in Pakrac and Lipik and Novska. That is to say, that Prijedor was being defended at the battlefield in Croatia. He never gave precise logical explanations as to why. He insisted that as many people as possible be mobilised and wage war against Croatia in order to defend Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, didn't it have to do with the fear that Croatian forces would come across the border and attack Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Because the Serb territory had already been rounded off in Croatia and a Serb parastate was created in that area so I don't think there was any military fear involved. However, this is a matter for military assessment and I am not an expert in this field.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like to you look at -- I'm going somewhere else again -- look at P1158, please. What you have before you there, sir, is indicated to be a conclusion adopted by the assembly of the Republic of Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina on 26 January, 1992, with a signature and stamp --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, sorry, that's not the one. Exhibit P1158?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 19th of February, Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina addressed to the municipal boards. Can you give us the Stakic number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can give you a disclosure number, 282. I can give you an ERN number, 01 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was it used in Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think so. 01107499 is the ERN number on the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The same document we have is like the one you have.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Try P102.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How come you've got all this mix-up, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it probably has to do with a -- I'm not going to make any -- these -- these exhibit numbers are entered into our data base system by people we can get to do that voluntarily mostly and they sometimes make mistakes and it appears we've run into two of them today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make sure that we have -- could you put it on the ELMO, please? And Mr. Ackerman, please check through the ELMO that we are talking of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Does that have an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: P102. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 26 January, 1992, assembly of the Republic of Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina and I'm just referring to that first paragraph, sir. "The decision to hold a referendum for the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which would be a basis for transforming Bosnia and Herzegovina into an independent state, was adopted in an irregular manner and without the presence of the Serbian deputies. As an act by the legal representatives of the Muslim and Croats peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it can be binding only on members of those two peoples. For the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina, this decision is invalid and directed against their existential interests." Do you understand what that means, directed against their existential interests?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the wording and interpretation that was given by the SDS. The parliament or rather we in parliament did not understand the decision of parliament in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Understand I'm only asking you about that last phrase, what does it mean, directed against their existential interests? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only interpret this sentence but again, I say that this is an interpretation of this decision by Serb politicians. There were also Serb opposition politicians who viewed this decision quite differently, the one that was controversial, as far as the SDS is concerned. And on the other hand, both groups of politicians belonged to the same people, to the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Does that phrase have legal significance, "Against their existential interests" that you know about?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it does not have any legal significance, because a certain number of Serb MPs left the parliament of their state in an unconstitutional way and they declared some kind of parallel parliament, and they adopted their positions. This is the actual situation, the factual situation, as it was viewed by the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If you're asking me what the sponsor of this text meant when drafting the text, I really cannot go into interpreting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. I'm finished with that. In Stakic you were shown a document and I hesitate to say what I think its exhibit number is but I believe it's Exhibit number P227.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If that's the gazettes, the Banja Luka gazettes, that's 227.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One issue, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can see it's not. What's the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I really don't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not going there, judge. It's the -- it's that document that we've talked about over and over and over signed by Lieutenant Colonel Milorad Sajic which --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That is part of it, it's part of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it's 227.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the only part of that, sir, that I have any interest in is in this decision by Sajic. He said, "A curfew is to be introduced on the entire territory between 2200 and 0500 hours except for members of the police, the military police and the Serbian Territorial Defence." And I take it you recall being asked about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't think there is any point giving it -- unless you give it to me and I'll tell you where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember being asked about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, front page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I cannot actually recall everything because I testified in the Stakic case for 39 hours. I spent 39 hours in this courtroom. So it's very hard for me to remember certain things but I know generally speaking that these topics were tackled as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you grateful that I'm not keeping you here for 39 hours or not?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have a look at the document, try and remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 4, a curfew is to be introduced. And you were simply asked by Ms. Korner if that curfew actually took effect. That's page 4590 of the transcript. And your answer was, "Yes, it did." And then you said, "I was not in Prijedor or Banja Luka at the time. I didn't go to Prijedor or Banja Luka in the evening hours, and that you know that it was put in effect because there were announcements on the radio or TV to the effect that movement was restricted. But you personally couldn't see it for yourself." So the fact is you don't know whether that went into effect in Prijedor or not, do you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not the way it is. I know that it came into force on the 30th of April. That is to say before the date that is mentioned here, namely when the Serbs carried out a military coup and took over power. So the authorities, the officials and people from the party were informed that a curfew had been imposed in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's all I need to know about that. At page 4871 of your Stakic testimony, in late 1991, early 1992, many persons were trying to leave Prijedor, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And those people included Serbs who were leaving Prijedor; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, but I know about the non-Serb population that was prevented from leaving. That is why some people came to complain. They came to the government authorities to complain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in many cases, though, in January and February, both Serb and non-Serb people were successful in leaving the municipality, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you said was, "However, as early as March, it was no longer possible because the Serbs in the Omarska and Banja Luka areas started to return passengers who were trying to leave by bus, and in April, it was completely out of the question," referring to the effort to leave. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By bus or other regular means of transportation, it was impossible to leave. If such attempts were made, then these persons were robbed and turned back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like to go into private session for just a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you to look at one more document and we'll be finished. The document is DB110. And what this is, sir, it's the minutes of an extraordinary session of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly of 14 February 1992, and this is a session of that assembly that you attended, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the date is the 17th of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Hmm. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I need a clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The translation is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I have the B/C/S original here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says 17 February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It does show indeed 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, so it just got it wrong on the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, sir, what I want to do is refer you to -- in your version, it would be a page with the ERN number P0053073.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the English version, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 20, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what you see there is a speech that you made.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us generally what the discussion that was being had that day was about?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that day, the request of the SDS for calling extraordinary parliamentary elections was discussed. I do not remember this in great detail but I know that this was the basic request of the SDS, because the SDS had already brought the parliament into blockade and somehow agreement was reached to have this session of the assembly held and then a discussion was held. The SDS thought that there were no normal conditions for holding elections, that there were problems, that they had to be resolved rather than have new elections held, and in this way, lose a month or two. That was the core of the discussion at this session.
