Individually, who said what is something I can hardly remember now, at least not in greater detail but we have got the minutes and perhaps I can comment upon that, if I manage to remember what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what -- I'm trying to do this as quickly as possible because I want to finish with you. What I would like to do, just to make it a little quicker, I think, is to have you look at that speech you made, there on the page I referred you to, and just read through it to yourself, just read it yourself, don't read it out loud because that will take longer and then just kind of tell the Trial Chamber the essence of what you're saying there, what does it mean, what's it about? Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading. I've finished, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Just tell us, essentially, what it is you're talking about there. What does all that mean?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what it means is the time saying that some other things should be accorded priority over extraordinary elections. That is the thrust of what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look, then, at the next thing that you said, which is just right after it, very little short paragraph there. What you said there was, "I will tell you about the elections Mr. Mutic. I ask you in your capacity as a professional journalist and as an assemblyman not to talk to me in this way." That's first. And second, "I perfectly understand you because it is unpleasant to have some fundamental and essential things said in your face from this floor. It was Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Izetbegovic, a gentleman from the HDZ who had agreed to hold by-elections even before the last elections and they confirmed it when they met at the opposition's initiative ten days ago. You may call your headquarters and check." Who was Mutic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a journalist with Kozarski Vjesnik who at the same time sat on the municipal parliament, municipal assembly, and he was commenting as I was speaking. There were some interjections on his part, and I reacted to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It appears from your reaction that were you taking the position that what he believed to be the case was simply not true. Is that a fair reaction?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, now I've lost you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You seem to be saying, when you in your second little speech there, with regard to Mr. Mutic, that what he apparently had been saying was not true because you told him that you could call your headquarters and check.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean the SDS had asked for extraordinary elections in the municipality of Prijedor. At the republican level, talks were already being conducted to have, extraordinary elections organised a few months later. So that was, as a matter of fact, the opposition's proposal to nationalist parties. And I know that there was an agreement, an understanding in principle, to hold those extraordinary elections, and I thought that we should wait for that particular moment rather than use this particular session to call the extraordinary elections at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what was it you were talking about with regard to blocking the assembly? What does that mean, "Blocking the assembly"?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. You used the language in here about blocking the assembly. Let me refer you to it just so -- because I want you to know what I'm talking about. Look at P0053102, sir, and in the English, it's page 37. And what you say there is, "It is my suggestion to bring this session to an end. In addition to what I said earlier I wish to say that we should avoid finding all kinds of pretexts and ways of blocking this assembly. I see it like this. We have a house, the door to is locked and now we want to pull down the house because we can't enter it. We have the key in our hand now. All we have to do is insert it into the lock, enter the house, and work normally. I repeat, the assembly is unblocked." What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initial SDS request for that particular assembly was that it should be dissolved and that extraordinary elections should be called. Our request was for the assembly to continue its work and to face up to the chief and the major problem at the time. And the discussion was very long, there were very many interventions and we managed to persuade a certain number of SDS assemblymen and of course other councilmen that the assembly should continue as it was rather than to take a decision to dissolve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the SDS was actually trying to have a brand new election hoping they might do better the next time?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was their interpretation -- well, no. I don't know why, because they did not say why. They simply said that such an assembly could not work properly and that they were after extraordinary elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Sejmenovic, have a nice trip home and thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you even try to leave this courtroom, you have another series of questions upon re-examination by the Prosecution. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, I'd like you to have back, please, the document DB108. Is that the B/C/S version? Yes, right. Now you were asked a number of questions about this yesterday morning. I don't think you told the Court exactly what these records are. What are they records of? They are obviously records of meetings but meetings of who or what?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks to me like the minutes put together by the Territorial Defence in Kozarac, because the Territorial Defence is the most frequently used word.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We know that you attended at least one of these meetings because we see what you say and your attention has been drawn to what you said. Before I take you to other entries I'd just like you to tell the Court this: What was the general mood at the meetings which you attended? In other words, what was it that, above all, the Territorial Defence in the Kozarac area was seeking to achieve?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence in Kozarac was seeking to remain within the -- to remain the part and parcel of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and insisted on the laws which governed its functioning before. That is if we are talking about the formal aspect of the question. If you're talking about its practical aspect, people were trying -- were trying to provide for these legal possibilities, but in view -- but they were living in tremendous fear and under serious psychosis. Sorry, the Territorial Defence therefore had -- did not have any military potential that would be adequate given the time and the adversary force and it tried to do its best within this short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was it the intention of the Territorial Defence of this area to start a war, an armed resistance, against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no way. There was no such option in play.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to look at just a few of -- your attention was drawn to some of the things that were said. I want to look at some of the other things, please, just a few. On the 30th of April, Kemo Fazlic spoke, saying "Is there a plan? No. Kozarac will not be defended by arms. Therefore everything should be undertaken before opening fire, wisdom is needed." Who was Kemo Fazlic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there was a man called Kemo Fazlic in Kozarac but what office he held and I don't think I personally know him. Perhaps if I saw his photograph, then perhaps I might recognise him, but as it is, I just can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then someone called Ilkan stated, "They will use these reserve soldiers as provocateurs, therefore there should be no response to the first shots." Now, on the same page, we can see that the -- under item 1, "The issue of the ultimatum for surrendering weapons, no surrender but we shall only respond if attacked." Two, "The issue of the members' insignia," and then three, "The delegation." Now, you don't know about Kemal Fazlic. Islam Bahonjic, about whom you were asked, first of all, who was he?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've mentioned Ilkan. Ilkan was the President of the Kozarac SDA. Islam Bahonjic was also a councilman in the municipal assembly. Islam Bahonjic came from the Kamicani SDA, another councilman in the municipal assembly, and I think he was also a member of the Territorial Defence, if my memory serves me well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Islam Bahonjic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed, and from what I heard, from others, in a horrible way. He was for a long time agonising.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just tell us where was he killed, from the information you received?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People in the Omarska camp told me that he had been tortured there, butchered, and that he took several days to die.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next, Becir Medunjanin?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Becir Medunjanin was the municipal secretary, that is head of the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence and another SDA official in the municipality of Prijedor, representing the territory of Kozarac because he lived there and he was also on the local SDA board in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you remember what sort of age he was?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have been around 45, 50 maybe.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he had a son?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had two sons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was one of them a man named Anes Medunjanin?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Yes, his elder son was Anes Medunjanin and I knew him well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Becir Medunjanin?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed in Omarska too, and his wife was also killed in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, Ilko Memic [phoen], do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the President of the local Kozarac SDA and a councilman in the municipal assembly in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He managed to leave the area on the eve of the war, supposedly using some private connections, and then he travelled through either Bosanska Gradiska or Lubica or some such place. That was the last thing that I'd heard about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look very quickly, then, at a few other entries in these records? Could you go to the next -- I think -- it may not be the next page. It's the 2nd of May entry, item number 3, miscellaneous. "A lot of our people carry out --" this is somebody called Nasib speaking. "A lot our people carry out acts of provocation. Fazlic and Hasan Didin yesterday fired in order to provoke. The police should immediately take such people to the police station and disarm them."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait one moment, Ms. Korner. Yesterday or the day before yesterday, I don't remember, he did point out that the words "in order to provoke" did not show up in the original B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's quite right. I've got it here. In fact the other question I wanted to ask was this, the only question I wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was just pointing this out to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right. I'd forgotten he said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was your view of anybody who set out to provoke the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had all this -- we had decided to prevent any kind of provocation, and of course, all those who were in charge, either in the Territorial Defence or the police, endeavoured to prevent and prevented such provocations, of course. Needless to say there were such cases. Somebody gets drunk and fires shots, then of course, one can intervene only when it comes to the consequences of that. And of course, there were shots fired, not too many, but you could hear them at times, although in that area, we were surrounded by other areas where the firing never stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to look at just two other entries, please. Could you find the entries for the 6th of June, a meeting at which you were present? Just before we move on, you said that you were surrounded by other areas where the firing never stopped. What areas did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The areas around Kozarac, with the Serb population, literally this whole belt, practically the whole belt around Kozarac, from all sides. And there, there was shooting, which never stopped, and it had gone on by that time for several months. That is frequent shots, with or without reason, and it was happening as of the time that people started coming from the fronts in Croatia and especially after the 5th Kozara Brigade came to quarter in the territory of the Prijedor municipality, because soldiers, the Serb soldiers, when going from the barracks home, would take their weapons and ammunition with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we look, then, just very briefly at an entry from the -- dated apparently the 6th of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's actually another mistake, Ms. Korner. It should be 6th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, 6th of May. I was actually going to say it must be a mistake. 6th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where we see under the agenda and then miscellaneous, one, "Vahid: We have established the peace headquarters consisting of members taken from all parties operating in the area." And then Mr. Hamdija Kahrimanovic stating, "I was pleased to be a mediator in a meeting similar to this, et cetera. We know who has put us in this situation, but there it is, and what we have to do is try and make peace prevail in the whole municipality." And so on and so forth. Now, you yourself attended a meeting with the SDS in the middle of May. Was this as a result of these discussions you had with other members of the Kozarac Territorial Defence and members of the non-Serb populations?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some representatives of the non-Serb population attended those meetings. However, when we arrived in Prijedor for that meeting, it was absolutely impossible to establish the kind of communication that we expected. Quite the contrary. The President of the SDS refused to talk pending the arrival of the Colonel and the major. It was only after the colonel and the major arrived, they then started moderating the meeting and they had the main say during the meeting. There was not a single mention of the agreement in -- of the agreement in Kozarac. It was then that they said that they were the Serb army, and then the meeting unfolded and we've talked about it repeatedly here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Sejmenovic. That's all I want to ask you about that document. Now, next, I'd like to you have a look, please, again, at a very short part of the video that Mr. Ackerman played you yesterday, which was the discussion about the takeover of the Kozara transmitter, and it was put to you by Mr. Ackerman that there was throughout all the interviews and all the credits that people were being given for their efforts in that regard, not once did we hear the name Brdjanin, did we? And you agreed. But I just want to play one small portion of what one of these people were saying, and it's been --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's been set up already. There is a transcript which Your Honours were given, if I can have it for a moment. It's P1533, but I'm -- no, I'm sorry, it's P1532, but it was S151. But I'd like, if possible, the interpreters just to interpret that short passage. Perhaps we can play it. Could somebody make sure that Mr. -- It's on. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] My war diary says Thursday, 31st of July, 1991. It's raining. Veljko Milankovic is arriving. In three sentences he briefs us about the situation. He said, his face grave, "The transmitter must be taken."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, could we go on, sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] The preparations took two days. On Saturday, around 1600, we prepared vehicles, people, uniforms, and in the civilian uniform, we went to Gradipa [phoen] where they were waiting for me as the commander, and headed for Europa. There, the politicians of the then AR Krajina, Bosnian Krajina, were waiting for us, and they in a few words explained to us the political significance of the takeover of the transmitter. Here, we changed into uniforms, with the insignia of the Krajina police, and we came -- we fetched up here in cars, and an engineer Branko, was already waiting for us. He had been briefed about the whole situation. We opened the gate. Veljko went in first and were followed by Mr. Mladen Sahaba [phoen] and they were followed by Zuti.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all. Thank you. I don't need any more of the video. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sejmenovic, all I want you to confirm is that as the interpreter interpreted it to us you were listening, I think, that what was stated by this gentleman -- I'll start that again. Mr. Sejmenovic, the man we were watching was a man called Desic, Ratko Desic, but can you just confirm that what he said was, "When we reached the Europa," which I assume is a hotel of some kind, "We were met by politicians of the then Autonomous Region of Krajina, that is Bosnian Krajina, who explained to us in short the political importance of the relay takeover."

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is precisely what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, finally, Mr. Sejmenovic, you had -- you were given a copy of the CSB report on Trnopolje or the report by Mr. Drljaca on Trnopolje and what he had to say about it and were you asked what your views were. I want you to please listen to some other descriptions of Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first, I thought, was a document that I'd put it through Mr. McLeod, but I hadn't and it will be going -- it was a letter written by Mr. Mayhew and I'm not -- I don't think we need trouble to give the witness the copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, can you just listen to this description, please, because were you asked about the machine-gun emplacements. This is a description written at the end of August, beginning of September. "Approximately 1600 male refugees, again almost all Muslim, are held there for their own safety, according to the Bosnian Serb authorities, although some officials claim the refugees are free to leave. However, small sandbagged military guard posts on the edges of the centre face inwards." Now, I don't know how closely you saw those machine-gun emplacements, Mr. Sejmenovic. Were you able to see whether the guns faced inwards towards the camp or out?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't know that this is proper redirect, because it's based upon the proposition that I was trying to prove something different and in fact what I proved was that the guns faced inward so I don't know why there is a redirect on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understood --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I asked him to mark the places were the guns were and which direction they were facing and actually where he came into the camp he came in between those two machine-gun nests that he identified, and he doesn't know where any of the others are. So I just think it's improper redirect and it doesn't challenge anything that I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's fine by me. I understood the suggestion being that the guards, the military guards were there to protect the inmates from outsiders. I did not -- I did not understand Mr. Ackerman to be accepting, from anything he said to the witness, that the machine-guns actually faced in towards the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's the way they were drawn. It is still my contention, however, Your Honour, that they were there to protect the people on the inside and that's why the commander of the guards there wanted to find out how he got into the place, not how he got out of the place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any way, let's proceed with the question. I think it's perfectly in order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Sejmenovic, can you remember whether the machine-guns faced in or out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He also said yesterday that he didn't know where all the machine-gun nests were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree. I just want to know if he saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So those that you saw with your own eyes, where were they pointing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some were pointing inside. Some were pointing outside. Your Honours, by your leave, Captain Slavko was not interested in how I got in. He was interested, I quote, in how I was getting in and how I was getting out repeatedly. Because I got in, got out, and got in again. I added this, if it can assist you in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, just -- yes, Your Honour, I don't think in fact I was going to put part of what was in the OSCE report, but I don't think --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, I mean in just a few sentences, without me putting anything to you, how would you sum up the conditions in Trnopolje for the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment when I was there, women, children and old people were being brought in, as well as men who were of age, but the two were separate. Women, children and some old men were evacuated, as well as some men who had enough money to pay, and they were evacuated by buses or trains. Some men were taken away, beaten up, interrogated, within the premises of that particular complex. Others were taken away and killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, thank you very much. That's all that I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, before you sit down, this -- what are we going to do with this report?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's going to be admitted through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Some other witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Another witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And with regard to the other documents that were circulated earlier?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was going to put part of it, again they are going to come in through same witness. When I had another look at it, I decided it wasn't going to take us much further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what I'm going to do is hand them back to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, should we take them back altogether and then hand them out

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To confuse us. Do I take it that you're ready with your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're finished?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any questions? Any questions? Mr. Sejmenovic, as I told you earlier, referring back to your testimony in Stakic, and considering that since I brought this up, you have been testifying again for over an hour and a half, are there any instances that you referred to in the Stakic -- in your Stakic testimony, or your testimony in Stakic, which are of significance, which are of importance, to which you were personally a witness, that you would like to point out to us, leaving apart, leaving aside, all the other information that you testified about or upon in the Stakic case, which you had come to know, knowledge of which you had acquired, as a member of the organisation you belonged to? Just the events that you witnessed personally which you think are of significance and which we ought to know that you testified upon because you knew the facts personally.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that everything that is important is what I have been asked during these five trials. I certainly would have recalled the important details when working with the Office of the Prosecutor, so I believe that I did not omit anything of importance related to Stakic. I said then that we had very few personal contacts. I observed his work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's going to be a bit too difficult to do this in the way Your Honour wants, but I think if I may, if I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- just take him through the major parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, you testified and you've testified over and over again, first of all, about your election to the assembly in Sarajevo, and the Prijedor Municipal Assembly. In both cases, you attended those assemblies, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You testified of your own knowledge what you yourself saw happened in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now I've understood the point of your question, Your Honour, so I can proceed on my own. I attended the meeting or rather the negotiations. I attended the meeting or rather the negotiations with the Serb Democratic Party and the officers who put an ultimatum before us. I attended the sessions of the municipal assembly, some sessions that were attended by Mr. Stakic too. I attended meetings at the local commune. I observed the shelling of the other part of Prijedor, that is to say, the part of the hills in Hambarine or rather the fire that broke out then. I watched the shelling of Kozarac and later on physically I got very close to Kozarac by bicycle myself and I viewed this from a very short distance. I also viewed the shelling of the refugees who were moving out by the village of Sivac. I also saw the men being taken away, either in vehicles or on foot, in the directions of Kozarac or Trnopolje. I personally watched five men being taken out of the camp of Trnopolje, five men who never returned afterwards. I personally saw a man who was taken away in the morning and who came back in the afternoon, after having buried these five corpses. I saw the Serb civilians entering the camp of Trnopolje and I saw them talking to some men who were non-Serbs and who were taken out the next day and killed. I saw a great many things, if we are considering what I saw personally, and I can go on enumerating these things that I saw personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can stop there. I think we can stop there. There being no further questions, your testimony comes to an end here. Once more, I would like to thank you for having accepted to come over and give evidence in this trial. I know that this is the fifth time, the fifth case, that you have testified in, so I thank you once more. You will be attended to by the organisation staff of this Tribunal to help you return to your country and you will now be escorted by our usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think in the course of my examination, I used Exhibits DB107 through DB115 and I just want to make sure that they are all offered and admitted properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure you used them all to tell you the truth. I seriously doubt that, but if you want to have them admitted, I see no point in arguing about it. I will have them admitted, because they are all relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, according to Ms. Gustin's log, used was DBs 107, 108, 109, 112, 113.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He may have used 110 as well. If I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I certainly used 111. We went through that at great length. I certainly used 110 because that was the one that had the wrong date on it and we fixed that. I think I used them all, Judge, whether I did or not I am offering them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will not argue with you about that but they are being admitted, all of them, as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can we just deal with the exhibits part before we deal with something else, Mr. Ackerman, sorry. As far as tendering of the Prosecution side of this, the transcript we'd ask to be tendered as 1533. Now, regrettably, with all sorts of exhibits, some which have not been tender, some which -- I mean they've all been tendered, but some have separate exhibit numbers, but we've given the schedule to Ms. Chuqing and I think we just have to exhibit the remaining ones as P1533/ whatever the S number is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And she's just going to have to work out what they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I mean, it's not easy, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We have provided a cross-reference schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it could be worked out before the next time we meet, before the next sitting. Is there anything else before we wind up for the day, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The case stands adjourned until Wednesday. I take it we'll hear the evidence of Lord Ashdown.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I think we are Wednesday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wednesday morning, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We got a message originally saying that he had to leave by noon. We pointed out this was somewhat difficult and I gather he can now stay until the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you all and have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 4th day of December, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.38 p.m.,
